title: The Formal Accessibility Audit 📋
description: Structure a professional audit: scope, methodology, sample pages, report format, and WCAG success criteria mapping.

slides.title: What Is an Accessibility Audit? 📊
slides.content:
An audit is a systematic evaluation of a product against WCAG success criteria. It results in a report that:

- Lists all issues found.
- Maps each to a specific WCAG criterion.
- Describes impact and remediation.

Common audit levels:
- **Full audit**: every page and component.
- **Baseline audit**: representative pages covering all templates and components.
- **Spot check**: a specific feature or flow.

quizData.question: What is the output of a formal accessibility audit?

options.text: A detailed report with issues, WCAG references, and fixes

quizData.explanation: A proper audit document lists all violations with evidence and recommendations.

slides.title: Step 1: Define Scope & Sample 🎯
slides.content:
Choose a representative set of pages that covers:

- Home page
- Content page (article, product)
- Interactive pages (forms, search results)
- Modal/overlay states
- Logged‑in vs. logged‑out
- Error states (404, validation errors)

If the site uses a component library, test each component individually.

slides.title: Step 2: Select Audit Methodology 🧪
slides.content:
Combine:

- **Automated scan**: run axe, Lighthouse, WAVE on each sample page.
- **Manual checks**: keyboard, zoom, contrast, focus order.
- **Screen reader**: test at least one desktop and one mobile screen reader.
- **Code review** (optional): inspect source for semantic HTML, ARIA.

Check against WCAG 2.2 AA as the standard (or your target level).

quizData.question: Why do you need a sample of pages instead of just the home page?

options.text: The home page is the most important
Different templates and components have different issues

quizData.explanation: An e‑commerce home page may pass, but the checkout might fail miserably.

slides.title: Step 3: Document Findings 📝
slides.content:
For each issue, record:

- **Location**: URL and element/component.
- **Description**: what is wrong.
- **WCAG Criterion**: e.g., 1.1.1 Non‑text Content.
- **Impact**: High / Medium / Low.
- **Recommendation**: how to fix it.

A common format is a spreadsheet, but tools like **Accessibility Insights** generate structured reports.

quizData.question: An issue is found where a search button has no label. Which WCAG criterion is violated?
quizData.explanation: A button without an accessible name fails 1.1.1 (if image) and 4.1.2.

slides.title: Step 4: Prioritise & Track 🚦
slides.content:
Categorize issues by severity:

- **Critical**: blocks users from completing tasks (e.g., missing form labels, keyboard trap).
- **High**: significant difficulty (e.g., poor contrast, missing alt text on important images).
- **Medium**: inconvenience (e.g., skipped heading level).
- **Low**: cosmetic (e.g., redundant link text).

Track fixes in your bug tracker; link to the audit reference.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use a template
Create an audit spreadsheet with sheets for each WCAG principle. This ensures thoroughness.
